title: Mediterranean and MIND Diets Linked to Better Cognitive Performance
excerpt: A pooled analysis of 17,368 participants across Europe and the US found continuous Mediterranean, DASH and MIND diets tied to sharper thinking — but only MIND held up over time.
body:
• A new paper in The Journal of Nutrition pooled individual-level data from 17,368 participants across 8 cohorts in Europe and the United States, comparing seven popular healthy dietary patterns head to head.
  • Looked at as a snapshot, higher adherence to the continuous Mediterranean diet was linked to better global cognition, while DASH and continuous Mediterranean diets were linked to better executive function.
  • Tracked over time, only the MIND diet — assessed in three US cohorts — stayed linked to better executive function; the other patterns did not show longitudinal benefits.
  • Practical takeaway: leafy greens, vegetables, berries, whole grains, nuts, olive oil, beans and lentils; less fried food, butter, pastries and processed red meat — with physical activity alongside for real long-term benefit.

The news

Certain healthy diets are linked to sharper thinking, but the link is more fragile than headlines suggest. That is the measured conclusion of a new individual-participant-data meta-analysis in The Journal of Nutrition, in which US and European researchers harmonised data from 17,368 people across 8 cohorts to compare seven dietary patterns: the Healthy Eating Index-2020, the Alternate Healthy Eating Index-2010, EAT-Lancet, the traditional Mediterranean diet, a "continuous" Mediterranean score, DASH, and MIND (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay).

Viewed cross-sectionally — diet and cognition measured at the same point — higher adherence to the continuous Mediterranean diet was associated with better global cognition, while higher DASH and continuous Mediterranean adherence were associated with better executive function. But the authors stress that snapshot findings did not necessarily hold up over time: longitudinally, only the MIND diet, assessed in three US cohorts, was linked to favourable executive function.

Context & background

The study was a direct response to a gap flagged by the 2025 Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee, which weighed the evidence on dietary patterns and dementia risk and concluded there was not enough data to make a recommendation. With roughly 57 million people worldwide living with dementia and 10 million new cases diagnosed each year, the public-health stakes are enormous — and the research literature was a muddle of different methods, definitions, and populations.

The new paper's answer was harmonisation: standardise how diet adherence is measured across studies, pool the individual-level data, and test each pattern the same way. Lead author Natalia Soldevila-Domenech and colleagues published in The Journal of Nutrition (2026), with support from the Institute for the Advancement of Food and Nutrition Sciences' Cognitive Health Committee. Dietary intake had been assessed with food-frequency questionnaires, diet histories, or food records.

"It is likely that both diet quality and physical activity are important lifestyle factors for slowing down cognitive decline."

— Lyn Steffen, University of Minnesota

Impact & analysis

The cross-sectional versus longitudinal split is the crux — and the reason this paper is more useful than most diet headlines. A snapshot association can reflect reverse causation (people with sharper cognition may simply eat better) or shared lifestyle factors. That only MIND survived the longitudinal test is intriguing but narrow: three US cohorts, executive function only. And Steffen herself notes the sobering context — the nonsignificant longitudinal results for the other patterns line up with a large randomised trial of the MIND diet that found no significant cognitive difference versus a control diet.

The authors' own conclusion is appropriately modest: dietary quality "may support cognitive health but likely requires integration with broader lifestyle improvements for meaningful long-term benefits." In plain terms: food is one lever, not a shield. The MIND pattern itself is unglamorous good sense — leafy greens, berries, whole grains, nuts, olive oil, beans and legumes; less fried food, butter, sweets, pastries, and processed red meat.

Diaspora angle

There is a quiet resonance here for Indian kitchens. Much of everyday desi cooking already mirrors the MIND pattern's emphases — lentils and legumes, leafy greens like palak and methi, vegetables, modest meat — which is a more useful framing than importing a Mediterranean shopping list wholesale. The caution runs both ways, though: deep-fried snacks, sweets, and heavy ghee use sit on the wrong side of the same evidence. Gradual shifts — more greens and berries, less fried food — are exactly what the researchers say can still matter.

What's next

The harmonisation approach is arguably the paper's biggest contribution: a template for cleaning up a noisy field so future dietary guidelines can be built on comparable evidence. For readers, the honest message is that no diet has been shown to prevent dementia, but eating patterns rich in plants and low in processed food are associated with better cognitive performance — and they pair best with movement, sleep, and the rest of a healthy life.
